tx.t: In this lecture I will describe the Aral Sea, one of the biggest environmental disasters of the last century. The Aral Sea, between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, was once the fourth largest lake in the world.

From the nineteen sixties, water from the two rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, was taken to irrigate cotton fields. By two thousand and seven, the sea had lost about ninety per cent of its volume.
The fishing industry collapsed, and ships were left on dry sand near the town of Moynaq. The exposed seabed is now a desert called the Aralkum, where salty dust storms harm people's health.
Today, tree planting on the old seabed and a dam in the northern part have helped to restore some of the water.

tx.t: Today we look at how printing changed the world. Before printing, every book in Europe was copied by hand, usually by monks, which took months.
Around fourteen forty, a German goldsmith called Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press with movable metal letters. The famous Gutenberg Bible was printed around fourteen fifty-five.
William Caxton set up the first printing press in England in fourteen seventy-six. By the year fifteen hundred, historians estimate that more than twenty million books had been printed in Europe.
Cheaper books helped literacy spread and made it easier to share new scientific ideas.

By two thousand and six, the number had risen to two hundred and ninety-seven pairs, which shows that careful management can work.

It stretches for roughly two thousand three hundred kilometres. It is not one reef but a network of nearly three thousand individual reefs.

Warm water causes corals to expel the algae that feed them, which turns them white. This is called bleaching. Scientists say that rising sea temperatures are the greatest long-term threat to the reef.
